courseTitle: Ionic - Build iOS, Android & Web Apps with Ionic & Angular

cues.en: So what is Capacitor or Cordova?
I really want to mention this. In this course, we use Capacitor because that is a tool developed and
maintained by the Ionic team and therefore, we can pretty much rely on this being up-to-date and only
growing in popularity and feature richness over the time.
Cordova nonetheless is an alternative to Capacitor and historically, Ionic did use Cordova.
You could still use Cordova with Ionic 4 and the official docs of course are the way to go if
you want to
but here we'll focus on Capacitor
but nonetheless what are these two tools?
Well remember that we're building an app here with Ionic and Angular
and what we're building is a web app, that is why we're previewing it in the browser all the time, though
of course I did show you how you can run it on a real device too.
But if you do run it on a real device, you absolutely have to remember that your web app is basically
wrapped in a native app and that native app renders a web view with your app in it
and this native web view or this app and the web view in it is basically what's provided by Capacitor
or Cordova.
So these tools basically give you a native app shell, take your web app, wrap it into that and then build
a real native app out of this shell plus web app thing.
Now in this course as I mentioned, we'll use Capacitor and not Cordova but they both have this core philosophy
or idea but of course, just wrapping a web app on its own
isn't that helpful because when you're building a mobile app, you obviously have a bunch of native platform
APIs, so basically APIs you could normally use when you're building an iOS or an Android app with
the native languages for these platforms,
so with Objective C or Swift for iOS or with Java for Android,
these native platform APIs I'm talking about are things like using the camera or using a mobile payment or
anything like that.
Now of course, we want to utilize these APIs from our Ionic app as well
but keep in mind, it is just a web app wrapped into a native app and therefore Capacitor and Cordova
also provide a bridge to these native platform APIs. They give us Javascript methods we can call
which under the hood will basically translate to native API calls that allow us to tap into that camera
and so on and Capacitor does all of that by giving us a rich set of built-in APIs we can tap into
and we can also add plugins as a community and therefore we'll see more and more features being provided
over time and it gives us access to all these APIs through one single Javascript API we use from our
web app and through that single API where we call the same method, no matter where our app runs,
if that is in the web or on iOS or on Android, we can reach out to the iOS, Android and possibly web
APIs that are provided and that is also important.
Even if your app runs really just on the web, so not wrapped into this native app on iOS or Android
but in a browser on your Macbook or your PC, even then, modern browsers give you a lot of nice features
like access to the camera or autolocation with geolocation package and Capacitor basically gives you
access to all these features, no matter on which platform you are and if something should go wrong, so
if you are trying to use a certain feature that is not supported on the platform your app runs, it will
fail gracefully.
So that means you basically get a chance to recover, to provide an alternative, to provide a fallback
and that is also what we'll do in this course.
And one other important note, if you already have an existing app and you want to rebuild it with a Ionic and
Capacitor and in that existing app, you will use the bunch of Cordova plugins,
these are still supported by Capacitor and the official docs of Capacitor are the place where you can
learn more about that.
